title: Talking to yourself by name
hook: third-person self-talk helped people stay calmer under stress

segments.voice: Yesterday: volunteering and health, a real link with a catch, and the Sikh word seva. Your line was give an hour. Did your hour land on a real day? Day one thousand three hundred forty-five.

"Okay, Maria. You've done harder things than this. Slow down." A woman is saying it to the mirror in an office bathroom, five minutes before a job interview, half embarrassed in case someone walks in. It looks like a strange habit. Talking to yourself, out loud, and in the second person, as if you were somebody else. It turns out psychologists have tested that very habit, and the small change it makes, from I to your own name, is today's lesson.
screen: `"OKAY, MARIA. SLOW DOWN."` → `TALKING TO THE MIRROR.` → `FROM I TO YOUR NAME.`

segments.voice: First, the experiment. Ethan Kross and colleagues, writing in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, gave people a stressful task: give a speech, with very little time to prepare. Before speaking, some were asked to think through their feelings using I. Others were asked to use their own name and you. The name-users reported less shame afterward, and observers rated their speeches as better. Second, why it might work. The researchers call this distanced self-talk. Using your own name puts a little space between you and the moment, the same space you have when a friend calls with a problem. It can be easier to see clearly into a friend's trouble than your own. Your name borrows some of that wisdom. Third, an old version. In Psalm 42 the singer turns and speaks to his own soul as if it were someone else in the room. In the King James Bible: "Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted in me?" He doesn't scold himself. He asks, and then he answers with hope. Talking to oneself is old, and it can be gentle. Fourth, the fine print. This is lab research with a speech in a room, not a cure for every hard day. Distance helps with the moment; it doesn't replace help when things are heavy. And the voice matters. Calling yourself by name in the voice of a harsh boss is the inner critic with better grammar. The research and the psalm both point to the coach, not the critic. By name.
screen: `A SPEECH WITH NO TIME TO PREPARE.` · `DISTANCE: ADVICE AS IF TO A FRIEND.` · `PSALM 42: SPEAKING TO THE SOUL.` · then, large: `THE COACH, NOT THE CRITIC.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: coach yourself by name. Sit and let the breath settle. Bring to mind one thing ahead of you that feels hard: a conversation, a deadline, an appointment you've been dreading. Now, silently, speak to yourself the way a good coach would, using your own name. Your name, then something true and steady. You've prepared for this. Take it one piece at a time. Notice how the sentence sounds when it's addressed to you rather than coming from you. Some people of faith bring the same hard thing into prayer. The bell holds the time.
Talking to yourself by name. Distanced self-talk: your own name and you, the way you'd speak to a friend. Today's word.
screen: `TALKING TO YOURSELF BY NAME — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: by name. Today, the next time stress spikes, say one calm sentence to yourself using your own name, under your breath if you need to. Day one thousand three hundred forty-five.

howItsDone: Some people use distanced self-talk before stressful moments, quietly addressing themselves by name or as "you" to steady themselves, much as the Psalms speak to the soul.

trapdoor: what you thought: talking to yourself is a little odd.
what it means: using your own name and you, instead of I, helped people feel less shame and speak better under stress.
what a scholar hears: distanced self-talk, a form of psychological distance. the lab evidence comes from tasks like a short speech, and the tone of the self-talk still matters.
